title: Cross-Fitted Doubly Robust Inference under Stringent Gaussian-Balance Rerandomization
banked_reason: Authoritative D0.5 tier subfield: paper_score_ceiling 6.8 < 7.4 field floor, salvageable=false; independent main validity confirms stop. Math PASS and all five citations verified-attested; three positioning/ballast findings remain disclosed.
tldr: For the actual cohort-normalized balanced Gaussian design, the unchanged original cross-fitted MAR doubly robust estimator has a uniform oracle expansion, a derived Gaussian limit with estimator variance \(V(P)\), consistent fitted-score variance, and asymptotic \(.95\) Wald coverage. A deterministic public radius family is admitted when \(\sup_{a\in\mathcal A_n}\min\{(N_np_n(a))^{-1},N_np_n(a)\}\to0\). Dense acceptance uses annealed transfer; sparse acceptance uses the prescribed complete-balanced fallback, with total variation at most \(N_np_n\). This retains the polynomial corollary and covers every fixed exponential radius \(e^{-\gamma n}\), including \(\gamma=(\log2)/d\) and larger values. Separate nuisance consistency and \(\sqrt n\,r_{\eta,n}r_{\kappa,n}\to0\) suffice. The finite evaluated envelope takes the better of the two certified errors. The moving order-one expected-count window remains outside this sufficient theorem.
gap: Wang and Li (2026), Theorem 5 and Appendix B.3.1, justify learned MAR adjustment at a positive fixed gate; Section 9 identifies shrinking-threshold extensions as unresolved. Wang and Li (2022), Condition 2 and Theorem 3, control diminishing-imbalance linear inference through an acceptance-dominated approximation. Neither supplies the ordinary-risk learned-fold argument for the present actual normalized design.
fill: The full inference theorem replaces division by acceptance mass with a signed-fold risk bound and density-level oracle approximation. It retains the software score, original training records, empty-set fallback, and iid nuisance risk qualifications. A quantitative coverage question asks for evaluated constants and tails rather than additional learner assumptions.
